input:
Basis

This report sets out the design of an amine absorber for a gas treatment duty, and the basis on which the design rests is as follows. The design throughput is 15 t per day, and the removal duty is 97% of the key component in the feed gas. The materials basis is that wetted parts are in 316L stainless steel, and that statement is made here, in the basis, so that the materials discussion later in the report can refer back to it. The basis also fixes the frame within which the rest of the design is developed: the absorber is to treat the stated throughput continuously, the duty is expressed as a removal of the key component rather than as an outlet specification in absolute terms, and any matter that the design has not been able to settle is not hidden within the sizing but is instead carried openly into the risks section at the end of the report. It is worth noting that the basis does not attempt to fix every operating variable in advance; rather, it fixes the throughput, the duty, and the materials, and it leaves the detailed selection of internals and the detailed circulation arrangements to the sizing discussion, where they properly belong.

Sizing

The sizing of the absorber is governed by the need to bring the gas and the amine solution into sufficiently close and sufficiently prolonged contact for the stated removal to be achieved at the stated throughput. The column diameter is set by the gas and liquid traffic through the vessel: the diameter must be large enough for the traffic to pass without flooding and without excessive entrainment, and the liquid must be distributed over the cross-section so that the whole of the contacting volume is used. The height of the contacting section is set by the separation requirement, since the removal duty can only be met if the gas is exposed to enough contacting stages, or to an equivalent depth of packing, for the key component to transfer from the gas into the solvent to the extent required. The solvent circulation rate is the other principal sizing variable, because a higher circulation gives a greater capacity for the key component per pass, at the cost of a greater regeneration load elsewhere in the process. The sizing adopted is therefore a balance among diameter, height, and circulation, struck at the design throughput. The report does not resolve the behaviour of the column at throughputs well below the design value, and that question is carried forward as an open item rather than being settled here by assertion.

It should perhaps be explained that the sizing discussion proceeds in this way because the variables concerned cannot in practice be chosen independently of one another: a change in the circulation alters the loading of the solvent and the duty of the regeneration section; a change in the diameter alters the velocities of both phases and with them the closeness of contact; and a change in the height alters the pressure cost of passing the gas through the column. The design that is reported is thus a single consistent selection among these variables, and not a collection of separately optimised items.

Materials

The materials requirement is that wetted parts are in the stainless steel grade named in the basis. The parts concerned are those in contact with the amine solution or with the wet gas: the column shell and internals, the liquid distribution arrangements, and the associated wetted pipework and fittings within the battery limit of the report. Amine service is corrosive in character, and the selection reflects the need for the wetted surfaces to resist the solution, the absorbed component, and the products of solvent degradation that accumulate in service. Fabrication requirements follow from the selection: welds in wetted parts are to be made by procedures appropriate to the grade, and the finished surfaces are to be inspected before the equipment is put into service. Parts that are not wetted, such as external supports and cladding, are outside the materials statement, and the report makes no selection for them. The materials position is thus a single requirement, stated once, applied to the wetted boundary of the absorber and its associated items.

Risks

Two open items are named in this report, and neither of them is resolved here. The first is fouling. In amine service, deposits can form on the internals and on the liquid distribution arrangements, and fouling of that kind reduces the effective contacting area and raises the resistance to gas flow through the column. The rate at which fouling might develop in this service is not established by the design work reported here, and no cleaning interval is fixed. The risk is therefore carried as an operating risk: performance is to be watched in service, and a deterioration in removal or in pressure behaviour is to be read as a possible sign of fouling rather than being attributed at once to other causes. The second open item is turndown. The design is struck at the stated throughput, and the behaviour of the column at substantially lower throughputs has not been demonstrated: liquid distribution and wetting of the contacting surface can deteriorate as the liquid rate falls, and the removal duty may not be held at the bottom of the operating range. No turndown ratio is claimed in this report. Both items are left open deliberately. The design as reported is complete at its basis, and the two risks define the limits of what the design has established: fouling governs the durability of the performance in service, and turndown governs the width of the operating range over which that performance can be assumed.
target:
Basis

The design throughput of the amine absorber is 15 t per day, and the removal duty is 97% of the key component in the feed gas. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel; the grade is stated here, in the basis, and the materials section refers back to this statement. The basis fixes three things: the throughput, the duty expressed as a removal of the key component, and the materials of the wetted parts. Operating variables not fixed by the basis are settled in the sizing, and matters the design has not settled are carried into the risks section rather than absorbed into the sizing. The absorber treats the stated throughput continuously. The duty is a fractional removal, not an outlet concentration: compliance is judged on the share of the key component removed across the column, and the sizing is developed against that measure.

The basis is also the reference for later change: a throughput above the basis value, or a duty above the basis removal, is a new basis and not an extension of this design, because the sizing margins are struck against the stated figures and are not reported as spare capacity.

Sizing

Sizing is governed by contact between the gas and the amine solution: the removal duty is met only if the gas meets enough active solvent, over enough contacting length, at the design throughput. Column diameter is set by the gas and liquid traffic. The diameter must pass the traffic without flooding and without excessive entrainment, and the liquid must be distributed across the whole cross-section so that the contacting volume is used evenly. The height of the contacting section is set by the separation requirement: the gas must be exposed to enough contacting stages, or to an equivalent depth of packing, for the key component to transfer into the solvent to the stated extent. Solvent circulation is the remaining sizing variable. A higher circulation gives a greater capacity for the key component in each pass and is paid for in regeneration load outside the absorber. The adopted sizing is a balance among diameter, height, and circulation, struck at the design throughput. Sizing at the design point does not demonstrate behaviour well below that point, and low-rate behaviour is not settled in this section.

The contacting device is selected within the same balance: internals that give closer contact also give a higher resistance to gas flow, and the pressure cost of the contacting section is part of the sizing judgement, not an afterthought. Liquid distribution receives the same treatment. A distributor that spreads the solvent evenly at the design rate is part of how the height is made effective; height that the liquid does not reach, or that the gas bypasses, does not contribute to the removal. The rich solvent leaving the base of the column and the treated gas leaving the top are the two streams by which the sizing is judged in operation: the removal is read from the gas, and the solvent loading is read from the liquid, and a sizing that satisfies one reading while degrading the other has not met the duty. Regeneration sits outside the absorber, but the circulation chosen here fixes the load that the regeneration section has to carry, and the sizing records that coupling rather than treating the column as an isolated vessel.

Materials

Wetted parts are in the stainless steel grade named in the basis. The wetted boundary covers the column shell and internals, the liquid distribution arrangements, and the wetted pipework and fittings inside the battery limit of the report. Amine service is corrosive: the wetted surfaces meet the solvent, the absorbed component, and the degradation products that accumulate in the circulating solution, and the grade is selected against that exposure. Welds in wetted parts are made by procedures appropriate to the grade, and finished wetted surfaces are inspected before the equipment enters service. Parts outside the wetted boundary, such as external supports and cladding, are not covered by the materials statement, and no selection is made for them in this report. The materials position is one requirement applied to one boundary: the grade named in the basis, for the parts the process fluids touch.

Risks

Fouling and turndown are open items. Neither is resolved in this report. Fouling in amine service deposits material on the internals and on the liquid distribution arrangements; the deposits reduce the effective contacting area and raise the resistance to gas flow. The design work reported here does not establish a fouling rate for this service, and no cleaning interval is fixed. Fouling is carried as an operating risk: a deterioration in removal or in pressure behaviour in service is to be read first as a possible fouling sign, and the cleaning decision rests on that monitoring rather than on a date set at design. The monitoring that carries the fouling risk has to distinguish fouling from the other causes of a falling removal: a change in feed, a change in solvent condition, and a change in circulation can each move the same readings. The report therefore assigns the sign, not the diagnosis: deterioration opens an inspection question, and the inspection settles whether the cause is deposit on the internals or a process change that the design did not predict. Solvent condition is part of the same picture, since a degraded solvent loses capacity and can present, in the operating readings, much like a fouled column. Turndown is the second open item. The design is struck at the stated throughput, and behaviour at substantially lower throughputs has not been demonstrated. As liquid rate falls, distribution and wetting of the contacting surface deteriorate, and the removal duty may not be held at the bottom of the range. No turndown ratio is claimed. The design is complete at its basis, and the two open items mark its limits: fouling governs how long the design performance lasts in service, and turndown governs how far below the design throughput that performance can be assumed to hold.
